title: How to Turn an Existing Hobby Into a CAS Activity
summary: Learn how to turn an existing hobby into CAS with clear goals, evidence, reflections, learning outcomes, and a practical September-November plan.
body_markdown:
You can **turn an existing hobby into CAS** by making it intentional, adding a meaningful challenge, documenting your participation, and reflecting on your development. The hobby does not need to be new, but simply repeating your normal routine without goals or growth is unlikely to provide convincing CAS evidence.


September-November offers a practical structure. Establish a baseline in September, work toward a defined goal in October, and evaluate the result in November.


### Can an Existing Hobby Count for CAS?


Yes. The official[IB CAS subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/contentassets/5895a05412144fe890312bad52b17044/cas-2016-english-1st-final-web.pdf) explains that a CAS experience may arise from a personal interest, skill, talent, or opportunity for growth. Photography, football, baking, running, music, coding, chess, and dance can therefore become valid CAS experiences.


The important difference is **purposeful engagement** :


Ordinary hobby participation Strong CAS experience


Playing guitar occasionally Following a rehearsal plan to record three challenging pieces


Running the same route Training safely toward a distance or pace goal


Taking photographs for enjoyment Producing a themed series using unfamiliar techniques


Baking familiar recipes Developing new recipes and gathering structured feedback


Work used to satisfy a Diploma Programme course requirement cannot simply be relabelled as CAS. For example, artwork submitted for IB Visual Arts would not separately count, although an independent exhibition or community workshop might qualify. Confirm such distinctions with your CAS coordinator.


### Match the Hobby to a CAS Strand


The[IB defines the three CAS strands](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/creativity-activity-and-service/) as:


- **Creativity:** exploring and extending ideas that lead to an original or interpretive product or performance.
- **Activity:** physical exertion contributing to a healthy lifestyle.
- **Service:** collaborative and reciprocal engagement with a community in response to an authentic need.


Music, photography, writing, cooking, filmmaking, and design commonly fit Creativity. Running, dance, swimming, climbing, martial arts, and team sports usually fit Activity.


Service requires more than sharing your hobby. You must respond respectfully to an identified community need and create reciprocal benefit. One experience can involve several strands, but only claim strands supported by what actually happened.


### Add Meaningful Growth and Learning Outcomes


Ask: **What will be different from what I already do?** You could learn an unfamiliar technique, pursue a realistic performance goal, create a finished product, collaborate, mentor beginners, assume planning responsibility, or respond to feedback.


An experienced runner, for example, might follow an eight-week pacing plan, join a group, and investigate how sleep affects training. This introduces challenge without forcing the student to abandon a sustainable interest.


CAS students must demonstrate all **seven learning outcomes** across the complete programme, not in every individual experience. A carefully planned hobby will usually support two or three outcomes, such as:


- Identifying strengths and areas for growth
- Undertaking challenges and developing skills
- Initiating and planning an experience
- Showing commitment and perseverance
- Demonstrating collaboration
- Engaging with issues of global significance
- Recognizing the ethics of choices and actions


Choose outcomes honestly. Playing beside other people does not automatically demonstrate collaboration, while briefly mentioning a global problem does not prove meaningful engagement. The[RevisionDojo guide to CAS minimum requirements](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/understanding-the-minimum-requirements-for-cas-in-the-ibdp) explains how individual experiences contribute to the wider programme, which continues regularly for at least **18 months** .


### A September-November CAS Plan


### September: Investigate and Prepare


Record your starting level through a sample, time, photograph, performance, or skills checklist. Identify one area for improvement, choose a November goal, discuss eligibility with your coordinator, and decide what evidence you can collect appropriately.


A useful photography goal would be: “By the end of November, I will produce eight low-light photographs using manual settings and peer feedback.” This is clearer than “I will do more photography.”


### October: Act and Adjust


Follow a manageable schedule and document important turning points. Evidence might include dated drafts, training records, rehearsal clips, plans, correspondence, or participant feedback. Changing an ineffective plan can provide valuable evidence of problem-solving.


The[RevisionDojo guide to balancing CAS with schoolwork](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/balancing-cas-with-real-life) recommends setting fixed CAS periods and recording short reflections promptly rather than allowing documentation to accumulate.


### November: Demonstrate and Evaluate


Compare your final result with the September baseline. Explain what improved, which decisions mattered, what remained difficult, and what you would change.


Demonstration could involve a performance, portfolio, presentation, training summary, exhibition, recipe collection, or report. It should reveal learning rather than merely announce completion.


### Document the Experience Effectively


The CAS portfolio records engagement and reflection, but it is **not formally assessed with marks** . Quality is more useful than dozens of repetitive photographs.


For each significant stage, include evidence, brief context, reflection on a specific decision or difficulty, and a realistic next step. The[RevisionDojo CAS reflection guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-cas-reflections-what-coordinators-want) explains how to connect reflective claims to credible evidence instead of writing a simple diary entry.


### When Does a Hobby Become a CAS Project?


An ongoing hobby is normally a **CAS experience** , not automatically a project. Under the IB's[official CAS project guidance](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/creativity-activity-and-service/cas-projects/) , a project is collaborative, involves sequential CAS experiences, and lasts at least one month from planning through completion.


A hobby could become a project if several students organize a performance initiative, beginner training programme, community photography exhibition, or collaborative resource. A project may address one, two, or all three strands. The[CAS project versus experience guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-counts-as-a-cas-project-vs-a-cas-experience) provides a fuller comparison.


### Common Mistakes to Avoid


- **Claiming earlier participation retroactively:** use previous experience as a baseline instead.
- **Recording routine repetition:** add a goal, challenge, responsibility, or unfamiliar context.
- **Calling any helpful act Service:** identify a genuine need and consider reciprocity.
- **Claiming every learning outcome:** select only those demonstrated by evidence.
- **Writing reflections months later:** record meaningful insights while they remain fresh.
- **Skipping approval:** schools implement CAS and may have additional procedures.


For the wider relationship between experiences, projects, portfolios, and outcomes, see[RevisionDojo's overview of IB CAS](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-cas-explained) .


### Conclusion


To turn an existing hobby into CAS, keep the interest that makes it sustainable while adding a defined challenge, purposeful planning, appropriate evidence, and honest reflection. Use September to establish a baseline, October to act and adapt, and November to evaluate your learning. RevisionDojo's CAS guides and Jojo AI can help you organize evidence and develop reflection prompts without replacing your own thinking.
